title: Hot-standby vs traffic-split intake - Pelican Ventures
summary: Initial reliability and routing discovery to evaluate Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private for Pelican's multi-region product. Discussed hot-standby vs traffic-split strategies, KV cache behavior, SLO targets (p95/p99), security (KMS/SOC2/audit logs), and a scoped SE-led perf validation. Agreed next steps: send security pack, share prompt set, and schedule a performance test week of Apr 26.
topics: KV cache and prefix caching consistency
dedicated capacity sizing and burst policies
private VPC / on-prem considerations (KMS, audit logs, data residency)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-22 16:00 PT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luca (Redwood SE), Anika (CTO), Samir (Platform), Jules (SRE)

Summary: quick intake to align on Pelican's reliability requirements and decide between hosted/dedicated/private deployment patterns with emphasis on incident tolerance and routing behavior.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick intros, im maya, i'm the AE on this account. Luca is our senior se, he'll drive the perf bits.
[00:12] Anika: hi all, Anika here. We're doing a reliability pass for the new customer-facing assistant. main ask is 3 nines availability and <150ms p95 token latency for the synchronous flows.
[00:24] Samir: Samir, platform. we own the infra side. curious about hot-standby vs traffic-split approach, and how KV cache coherency works across regions.
[00:36] Luca: cool, will do. quick note — our tokens-latency numbers vary a lot by model and seq length; we should scope with your sample prompts.
[00:47] Jules: Jules — SRE — we also need audit logs, SSO, and KMS integration, and a runbook for partial degradation.

[01:02] Maya: perfect. high level: we typically recommend three patterns for multi-region reliability: active-active with traffic splitting, active-passive hot-standby, or region-local with cross-region fallback. each has trade offs for latency, cost, and cache behavior.

[01:30] Anika: can you unpack the hot-standby vs traffic-split? we keep reading different best practices and it's confusing.

[01:40] Luca: sure. traffic-split (active-active) means you send a portion of traffic to each region—good for lower tail latency because users hit nearest region; but it requires consistent prefix/KV caches or warm starts across regions to avoid cold-kv misses. hot-standby is where secondary regions are kept ready but not serving primary traffic most of the time—cheaper cache-wise but you need fast failover and warm-up strategies so user requests don't hit a cold cache on failover.

[02:10] Samir: how fast is "fast failover"? are we talking seconds or minutes? and what about in-flight requests and session stickiness?

[02:22] Luca: typical plan is sub-30s route switch at the DNS/load-balancer layer if you use region steering; but the big delta is the model KV cache — if your workload relies on long running chats with large k-v caches, regen cost can add 100s of ms per request until cache is rebuilt. we have two levers: proactive KV replication (more bandwidth/cost) or a short-lived sticky session that retries/pulls from origin. both are supported but require config.

[03:02] Anika: proactive KV replication — is that supported in hosted or only private/dedicated?

[03:12] Luca: we support cross-region prefix cache replication in Dedicated and Private setups more easily because you control the networking and bandwidth; hosted can do async cache warmers and checkpoint snapshots but cross-region replication at low latency is generally a Dedicated/Private feature. hosted has fallbacks and model variants to reduce cold-warm penalty.

[03:40] Maya: to add, many customers start hosted to validate UX, then move to Dedicated for predictable latency & cross-region replication when they have stricter SLOs. but some regulated customers go Private from day one for KMS/HSM and data residency reasons.

[04:00] Jules: what about circuit breakers and partial degradation? are those automatic?

[04:07] Luca: we have built-in circuit-breakers at the routing layer — policies can be set per-route: degrade to cheaper quantized model, increase timeout threshold, or return cached answer if available. also, automatic fallback routing can steer to other regions or to a lower-cost pool. you can set SLO-driven policies like "if p99 latency > X for 5m, route 20% to fallback".

[04:40] Samir: okay. illustrate for us: during a db outage in primary region, ideally we want read-only responses from cache and graceful degradation for new sessions. how would Redwood behave?

[04:54] Luca: if DB outage is just our cache store, we can serve from prefix caches in edge for recent sessions; if it's a full model-serving outage, route to secondary region or model-variant. we can return a structured prompt with an explicit disclaimer — e.g., "limited context, partial answer" — so app can show degraded UI. rule sets are configurable.

[05:20] Anika: latency SLOs: we target p95 < 150ms, p99 < 350ms. realistically, do you think Dedicated is necessary?

[05:32] Luca: for p95 150ms global it's tricky in hosted unless you pin to small local deployments; network egress plus tokenization cost matters. Dedicated with regional pools gives you predictable tail latency. We'll propose cluster sizing after we see your prompt set.

[05:50] Maya: and pricing: Dedicated adds a baseline commitment but predictable throughput usually reduces unit cost for high qps. we can provide estimates.

[06:05] Jules: security — we need KMS with CMKs in our cloud account, SOC 2 plus audit logs for every inference, and SAML SSO for the console. does Redwood support customer-managed keys?

[06:20] Luca: yes — Private (and Dedicated via dedicated control plane) supports customer-managed KMS and HSM. Hosted supports envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key in certain regions; we'll include exact matrix in the security pack. audit logs (per-request) are available for Dedicated and Private with retention configs. hosted retains logs but has retention limits unless you add an enterprise add-on.

[06:50] Anika: good. Jules: about routing policy granularity — can we do per-route SLO routing? for example, critical auth flows always go to dedicated pool while chats go to hosted.

[07:04] Luca: yes, route-level policies are first-class. you can mark routes as "critical" and pin them to clusters, or use SLO-based dynamic routing. we also have weight-based traffic-split if you want canary traffic between regions.

[07:20] Samir: what about sticky sessions for chat? we need session affinity so context stays in same region for performance.

[07:28] Luca: session affinity is supported via our routing tokens; it can be time-limited. if a region becomes unhealthy, affinity is broken and you'd either rehydrate context or fall back to a stateless reply. rehydration strategies vary by how you persist contexts (your DB vs our prefix cache).

[07:48] Anika: rehydration could be slow. can we pre-warm a subset of sessions on secondaries?

[07:55] Luca: yes — warmers can proactively seed KV caches in standby regions for a chosen set of users or sessions. that's a common hybrid approach: traffic-split for general traffic, hot-standby for VIP users.

[08:12] Maya: quick check: does Pelican have data residency constraints? any EU-only data or HIPAA?

[08:20] Anika: no HIPAA. Some EU customers require EU-only residency. we want the option to pin EU data to EU regions and audit access.

[08:30] Luca: Private or Dedicated in EU region can guarantee that. Hosted also has EU region options but for strict residency and KMS control, Private is recommended.

[08:45] Samir: about autoscaling — if we use Dedicated, does Redwood autoscale GPU pools quickly? and is bursting allowed for peak days?

[08:55] Luca: Dedicated supports autoscaling policies with min/max nodes and also a burst pool for short spikes. scaling is typically tens of seconds to a couple minutes depending on GPU availability. we also offer pre-warms for planned events.

[09:20] Jules: can you explain model-variants fallback? e.g., when latency spikes, do you switch to a quantized variant?

[09:28] Luca: exactly. you can define fallback chains: primary model -> quantized variant -> cached response -> canned response. each step reduces compute cost and latency but may reduce fidelity. you control thresholds.

[09:50] Anika: curious about SLO measurement — do you give token-level breakdowns? we want to chargeback and track per-route costs.

[09:59] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost, latency percentiles, per-route dashboards, and traces. that should let you do chargeback.

[10:10] Samir: are there any limitations for bursty short-lived chats on hosted? we have some flows with sudden spikes.

[10:20] Luca: hosted has throttles and rate limits to protect multi-tenant pools. for bursty predictable spikes Dedicated or Reserved capacity is better. we can add burst credits sometimes but that isn't as reliable as Dedicated.

[10:40] Anika: got it. can you walk through a sample incident scenario and routing behavior? say primary region node pool has a GPU crash and 60% reduction in capacity.

[10:52] Luca: incident path: autoscaler will attempt to create replacements; routing layer detects increased latency/error rates and will... (a) shift percentage of traffic to other healthy regions (active-active), (b) route critical routes to dedicated pool or pinned region, (c) apply fallback chain for degraded routes. If capacity drop is partial, you can enable graceful degradation: increase timeouts, bump fallbacks, and prioritize critical workflows.

[11:30] Jules: do you keep error budgets and alerts integrated with our pager?

[11:36] Maya: yes we can forward SLO alerts to PagerDuty/Slack and expose SLO metrics in Datadog.

[11:45] Samir: any known gotchas for long-running contexts with KV caches and region failovers?

[11:52] Luca: main gotcha is cold cache rebuild time and potential token cost for warming. also, if you try to replicate very large KV caches synchronously you'll pay bandwidth and complexity. so we usually advise tiering: critical keys replicated, others lazy-warmed.

[12:12] Anika: what's the expected lead time to set up Dedicated with three regions and cross-region replication?

[12:20] Luca: typical pilots are 2-4 weeks to provision clusters and run benchmarks; full production with replication and runbooks is more like 6-10 weeks depending on approvals and networking (VPC peering, firewall rules).

[12:38] Maya: for Private on-prem it's longer — packaging and security review add time. that timeline is normal.

[12:50] Anika: pricing: ballpark for Dedicated three-region baseline?

[12:56] Maya: we'll send a tailored quote but ballpark depends on GPU types and commitments. we'll include a 3-region hot-standby vs traffic-split cost comparison.

[13:08] Samir: can we run a perf validation against our prompt set? we want p95/p99 measured end-to-end including our upstream services.

[13:16] Luca: yes, SE-led perf test is standard. we'll run a 2-hour synthetic and a 1-2 day pilot with real prompts. we'll need your prompt corpus and expected qps.

[13:28] Jules: about observability: can we export raw request logs to our S3/GC?

[13:35] Luca: Dedicated/Private can push logs to your object store or SIEM; hosted can stream limited logs via an enterprise add-on.

[13:46] Anika: are you seeing any stability issues with cross-region traffic-split customers in prod?

[13:53] Luca: a minority. issues usually due to cache coherence expectations or opaque statefulness in the app. we mitigate with clear guidance: either make sessions stateless, implement sticky affinity, or accept partial warmers.

[14:10] Maya: ok let's go through action items and next steps.

[14:14] Anika: one more question — do you support FIPS endpoints for KMS and encryption?

[14:20] Luca: yes for Dedicated and Private in certain regions. we'll enumerate in the security pack.

[14:28] -- Meeting recap / action items --
[14:30] Maya: thanks, I'll capture action items.
action_items: Maya: send security pack + SOC2 evidence + matrix on KMS/FIPS by 2027-04-25
Luca: produce perf test plan and cluster sizing recommendation after receiving prompt set (due 2027-04-29)
Samir: share representative prompt corpus and expected qps, and list of critical routes (due 2027-04-24)
next_steps: Schedule SE-led perf validation (2h synthetic + 1-2 day pilot) week of 2027-04-26
Provide Dedicated 3-region vs hot-standby cost comparison and pricing estimate
Join Pelican security review meeting (Maya to arrange)
